Question 1

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=sin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj+tk at the point P(−1,0,32), valid for real values of u?

a
−i+32k+u(πj+k)
b
−i+32k+u(−πj−k)
c
−i+32k+u(πi+j)
d
−i+32k+u(i+πj+k)
e
−i−32k+u(πi+k)
Submit

decision.explanation: The k-coordinate gives t=3/2. Since r'(t)=π cos(πt)i−π sin(πt)j+k, we have r'(3/2)=πj+k. Thus option a is the tangent line through P. Option b describes the same line with the parameter reversed, since u ranges over all real numbers.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k$ at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2}),$ valid for real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
The point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t=-1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t=0 \\ t=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{3}{2}).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{3}{2}) & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,j+\,k \\  & =0\,i+\pi \,j+\,k \\  & =\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is

$$
R(u)=-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u\,(\pi \,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k$ at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2}),$ valid for real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
The point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t=-1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t=0 \\ t=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{3}{2}).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{3}{2}) & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,j+\,k \\  & =0\,i+\pi \,j+\,k \\  & =\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is

$$
R(u)=-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u\,(\pi \,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

c

decision.explanation: The tangent vector is r'(t)=⟨2t,3t²⟩. Perpendicularity requires r'(t)·⟨2,1⟩=4t+3t²=t(4+3t)=0. Since t<0, only t=−4/3 is allowed. Substitution gives r(−4/3)=(7/9,−37/27), so option c contains all qualifying points.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1\,,\,{t}^{3}+1⟩,t\in (-\infty ,0)$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨2\,,\,1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨2\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 2\cdot 2t+1\cdot 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(4+3t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-\frac{4}{3}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-\frac{4}{3}) & =⟨{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-1\,,\,{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{3}+1⟩=⟨\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$

content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1\,,\,{t}^{3}+1⟩,t\in (-\infty ,0)$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨2\,,\,1⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨2\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 2\cdot 2t+1\cdot 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(4+3t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-\frac{4}{3}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-\frac{4}{3}) & =⟨{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-1\,,\,{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{3}+1⟩=⟨\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$

Given the curve r(t)=⟨sin⁡t,3cos⁡t⟩,t∈[0,π) find all of the points at which r′(t) and r(t) are perpendicular.

a
 (1,0)
b
 (22,−322)
c
 (0,3) and (1,0)
d
 (1,0) and (32,−32)
e
 (0,3) and (22,−322)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨cos(t),−3sin(t)⟩, so r'(t)·r(t)=−8sin(t)cos(t). This vanishes at t=0 and t=π/2 within [0,π); t=π is excluded. The corresponding points are (0,3) and (1,0), giving option c.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,t\in [0,\pi )$ find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =0 \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in [0,\pi )$, the only solutions are $t=0$ and $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=⟨0\,,\,3⟩, \\ r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨1\,,\,0⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(0,3)$ and $(1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) & =0 \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨t3,t2−2⟩ at the point where t=3, valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨27,7⟩+u⟨9,7⟩
b
⟨9,1⟩+u⟨9,7⟩
c
⟨9,1⟩+u⟨27,6⟩
d
⟨27,7⟩+u⟨14,6⟩
e
⟨27,7⟩+u⟨27,6⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=3, the vector r′(3) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(3)+ur′(3),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(3): r(3)=⟨33,32−2⟩=⟨27,7⟩

Now, we calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(t3),ddt(t2−2)⟩=⟨3t2,2t⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=3: r′(3)=⟨3(3)2,2(3)⟩=⟨27,6⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=3 is
R(u)=⟨27,7⟩+u⟨27,6⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3},{t}^{2}-2⟩$ at the point where $t=3,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=3,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(3)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(3)+u{r}^{′}(3),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨{3}^{3},{3}^{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨27,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(3) & =⟨3(3)^{2},2(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨27,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=3$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨27,7⟩+u⟨27,6⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t-2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =⟨c\,,\,2c\,,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}2t-2=c \\ 2t=2c \\ 8-4t=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we obtain that $t=2.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=2.$
These values also satisfy the first equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{2}^{2}-2(2)\,,\,{2}^{2}\,,\,8(2)-2(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,4,\,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$
